item.title: NYC marathoner with 'heart for Jesus' remembered after tragic death for her faith, strength and charity
item.description: Athlete Rachel Apa, 24, was running the NYC Marathon to honor her late grandfather and raise funds to fight Parkinson's disease when rhabdomyolysis struck.
item.content:encoded:
Rachel Apa, 24, died on Sunday, Nov. 1, while running the New York City Marathon after succumbing to complications from rhabdomyolysis, a rare muscle condition.

Apa made it to mile 24 – just 2.2 miles from the finish line – before collapsing. She received immediate medical attention and was taken to Mount Sinai Medical Center, where physicians worked to save her for more than six hours.

The athlete was declared dead at around 9:40 p.m., according to a report from The New York Times.

NYC MARATHON RUNNER, 24, DIES JUST 2 MILES FROM FINISH LINE AFTER SENDING DAD CHILLING TEXTS

Rhabdomyolysis causes the muscles to break down when over-exerted, which leads to muscle death, according to Cleveland Clinic.

When this disintegration occurs, toxic components of the muscle fibers can enter the circulatory system and kidneys, which can cause kidney damage, essentially acting as poison to the body.

Apa graduated from Bucknell University, where she played Division I field hockey. Post-grad, she was a product manager for an electrical component company while also working on her MBA at Charleston Southern University (CSU).

In a tribute released Tuesday, the Christian university, where Apa began her graduate school education in August, said the CSU family "mourns the tragic loss."

HEALTHY ATHLETE HAD NO SYMPTOMS BEFORE MANDATORY HEART SCREENING REVEALED HIDDEN DEFECT

"Maxwell Rollins, assistant dean of graduate programs for the Nielsen College of Business, shared a recent class assignment where Apa stated her current mission was to take advantage of the talents and opportunities she had been blessed with to make an impact in any way she could in the lives of those around her," the statement reads.

Rollins shared about Apa, "She wrote that her desire was to demonstrate Christ’s love and character in both business and everyday life. Though she had just started her MBA at CSU, her passion for others and heart for Jesus will continue to serve as an inspiration for all our students."

CSU president B. Keith Faulkner added, "The loss of a vibrant young woman in the prime of her life is a sorrow no parent can imagine enduring. The Charleston Southern family is surrounding the Apa family, along with all who knew and loved Rachel, with our prayers and support."

"We will never fully understand why this happened to a young woman of such remarkable strength and character. Her final hours are forever marked by Rachel’s selfless dedication to helping others as she ran to raise funds in the fight against Parkinson’s disease."

MYSTERIOUS DISEASE SENDING YOUNG, HEALTHY TEXAS WORKERS INTO KIDNEY FAILURE

Faulkner continued, "We know that true peace comes only from the Lord, and we pray that His presence and comfort will be deeply felt by all who are grieving and by all whose lives were touched by Rachel’s extraordinary life and legacy."

Apa’s former field hockey teams also mourned her loss in tributes posted to social media.

Central Penn Field Hockey Club, where Apa was a member for nearly a decade before playing for Bucknell, posted that the family is "heartbroken by the loss."

"On the field, she played with intensity and determination," the club wrote. "She was competitive, serious about the game and gave 100% every single time, always with a smile and an unwavering commitment to her teammates."

"Watching her play was a beautiful thing. You could see the joy she carried every time she stepped on the pitch."

The statement continued, "Our hearts are with the Apa family, her CPFH and Bucknell teammates and their families, and everyone lucky enough to have shared the field with her."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Bucknell Field Hockey also posted on Instagram, featuring several photos and videos of Apa on the field alongside her teammates.

"Our hearts are broken for the Apa family, and we are deeply sorry for the unimaginable loss of their beautiful daughter, Rachel," the organization wrote in the caption. 

"The Apas are in the thoughts and prayers of the entire Bucknell Field Hockey family during this incredibly difficult time."

"Rachel’s spirit will be everlasting; her impact on the people and program will never be forgotten," the post continued. "We hope the Apa family can find some comfort in knowing she helped create something truly special here and will always hold a place in our hearts."

It went on, "We are sending you all our love, strength and support. Our entire Bucknell Field Hockey family is holding you close in our hearts."

Apa set out to run the marathon to raise money to fight Parkinson’s disease, in honor of her late grandfather.

On the Parkinson’s Champions fundraising website, Apa wrote what her grandfather meant to her.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"My grandfather was my role model growing up," she said. "He taught me to stay active, push my limits and embrace challenges, shaping my love for sports and movement.

"Later in life, he was diagnosed with Parkinson's disease, and I watched as the disease slowly took away the freedom to move that he once loved so much. He passed away in 2022, but the lessons he taught me continue to drive me forward."

She added, "I'm proud to run with Parkinson's Foundation Champions to raise funds and awareness for research, better care and a cure."

Rachel Apa raised more than $55,000 and counting for the cause.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

The Parkinson’s Foundation also released a statement in her memory, expressing that the organization is "saddened by the tragic passing" of Apa, who ran as a member of the Parkinson’s Champions team.

"Rachel’s decision to take on this challenge was deeply personal," the statement reads. "After watching Parkinson’s disease gradually take away the freedom of movement her grandfather once cherished, Rachel was inspired to honor his memory by running and supporting the Parkinson’s community."

"We admire Rachel’s determination and are grateful that she was part of our team. Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Rachel’s family, loved ones and fellow members of the Parkinson’s Champions team."

item.title: Utah student cited after physical altercation with College Republican caught on camera
item.description: Video captures a student appearing to say Republicans "should be shot" before allegedly tackling a College Republican at the University of Utah.
item.content:encoded:
A student was cited for simple assault and property damage after allegedly tackling a College Republican at the University of Utah during a confrontation over a campus poll about gender, moments after saying Republicans "should be shot in the streets," according to video of the incident and a university spokesperson.

The confrontation unfolded outside the university's Marriott Library, where members of the College Republicans had set up a whiteboard asking whether there are only two genders, The College Fix reported.

In a video shared Oct. 28 on X by University of Utah College Republicans officer Rylie Barnes, the student, identified by Fox 13 as Grace, is heard responding to a question about freedom of speech.

FORTY-FIVE PERCENT OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE CAN BE JUSTIFIED TO STOP HATE SPEECH, POLL FINDS

In the video, a person identified as a College Republican asks the student, "Do you believe we should have the right to freedom of speech?"

"No, I think Republicans should be shot in the street, personally," the student replied. The cameraholder says that it sounds like advocacy for violence. After a cut, the video then shows the person identified as a college Republican being knocked to the ground as he yells for the other student to stop; it's unclear how much time transpired between the remarks and the fight.

Fox 13 reported, "The student, who identifies herself as Grace, told FOX 13 News that the confrontation was a ‘set up’ and accused College Republicans of instigating and escalating it. She alleges that after she left the table, the Republicans followed her while saying ‘you are denying biology.’ She also says she was punched in the face during the fight."

In another interview, she said, "I believe I am a victim of transphobic aggression, and because the University protects the College Republicans and enables them to bully students, I was cited with these bogus charges."

CONSERVATIVE JEWISH ACTIVIST VOWS NOT TO BE SILENCED AFTER BEING ATTACKED ON UNIVERSITY OF MICHIGAN CAMPUS

Rebecca Walsh, communications director at the University of Utah, told Fox News Digital in a statement Tuesday, "On Oct. 27 at 12:52 p.m., University of Utah Police responded to reports of a fight between two students on Marriott Plaza."

Walsh continued, "While College Republicans were tabling on the plaza, another student approached the table and wiped off a whiteboard with their hand. To the side of the table, that student and one of the students tabling for the College Republicans started to argue about free speech and gender. The visiting student then assaulted the tabling student, knocking them to the ground and tearing their shirt. Police have identified the individual involved and issued two Class B misdemeanor citations--for simple assault and property damage."

She added, "The investigation is ongoing. Support and resources have been offered to both students."

Walsh also told Fox News Digital that the school could not disclose information about potential student disciplinary proceedings because of federal student privacy laws.

Walsh pointed to the university's student code of conduct, which prohibits threats, physical assaults, intimidation and other behavior that endangers the safety of students or members of the campus community, including threats made online.

Walsh said the police investigation remains ongoing and the university has offered the alleged victim support and resources through its Student Affairs team.

Walsh also emphasized that the university, as a public institution, protects the expression of differing viewpoints, including those of the College Republicans and student groups calling for the citations issued to Grace to be dismissed.

Walsh said the university is waiting for the outcome of the police investigation and reiterated that the university condemns threats of violence against anyone on campus and responds swiftly to such incidents.

The Utah Anti-War Committee issued a statement supporting who it identified as Amber Grace, writing, "Even though the College Republicans began this harassment, Amber is now facing misdemeanor charges of assault and property damage for resisting transphobia. Amber is a dedicated member of the Salt Lake community as an anti-war activist, and she did nothing wrong by speaking against hateful Republican rhetoric."

FOUL-MOUTHED ANTI-WAR PROTESTERS REPEATEDLY DERAIL HEGSETH'S REMARKS AT ARMY EVENT IN DC

The Anti-War Committee is calling on Salt Lake County District Attorney Sim Gill to "refuse the charges on Amber Grace! Speaking out against transphobia is not a crime."

Fox News Digital reached out to Grace, the University of Utah, the University of Utah College Republicans and Salt Lake County District Attorney Sim Gill for comment.

item.title: Texas Senate victor James Talarico lays out common ground with Trump, vows to 'work together'
item.description: Texas Senator-elect James Talarico says he wants to work with Trump on border security, a federal gas tax suspension and cutting housing regulations.
item.content:encoded:
Texas Democratic Senator-elect James Talarico said Wednesday he is ready to work with President Donald Trump on issues, including border security, lowering energy costs and cutting housing regulations.

Speaking on Fox News' "America’s Newsroom" after his victory over Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton Tuesday night, Talarico discussed several areas of potential cooperation with the president.

"I think there's a wide variety of issues that we could work together on," Talarico said.

JAMES TALARICO TORCHES BIDEN BORDER POLICIES IN STUNNING ATTACK AD AS PROGRESSIVE TRIES TO FLIP TEXAS BLUE

"Immigration is one of them. I think trying to pass comprehensive immigration reform that includes border security … give the president credit where credit is due. He has done a better job than the previous administration in securing our border," he added.

Talarico, who defeated Paxton by over ten points, said Congress must create more legal pathways for immigrants who want to come to the United States. He also expressed interest in working with Trump to reduce housing regulations, pointing to the president's background as a real estate developer.

"I also want to work with the president on housing. He's a builder, and we need to cut the red tape, the regulation that sometimes my party has been guilty of, so that we can build millions of new homes in this country," Talarico said.

TALARICO RALLY WARMUP ACT CALLS FOR ABOLISHING ICE, CONTRASTING SENATE HOPEFUL'S MESSAGE

Beyond housing and immigration, Talarico said he also wants to work with Trump to suspend federal gas and diesel taxes to lower fuel costs.

"He and I both support suspending the federal gas tax and the federal diesel tax," Talarico said, noting the move would lower fuel costs by "18 cents a gallon immediately."

Criminal justice reform was another area Talarico said offers common ground.

ENERGY SECRETARY WRIGHT SAYS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION OPEN TO SUSPENDING FEDERAL GAS TAX AMID PRICE SURGE

"Last one I'll mention is I agree with the president on the need to legalize marijuana and reform this broken criminal justice system," Talarico said. 

"These are just some of the issues that I agree full-heartedly with President Trump, and I look forward to working with him for all 31 million Texans."

Talarico also rejected the idea of pursuing political retribution in Washington, saying his priority would be delivering results for his constituents.

"I am not interested in retribution," Talarico said.

"The people of Texas did not elect me last night for retribution," he continued. "They elected me to deliver for them to make their lives easier and better and less stressful."

TRUMP CONGRATULATES DEMOCRATS AFTER DOMINANT MIDTERMS, SAYS HE LOOKS FORWARD TO WORKING WITH THEM

Trump had endorsed Paxton before Talarico’s victory, which gave Democrats their first U.S. Senate seat in Texas since 1988. On Tuesday night, Talarico announced his victory on X, writing simply, "We just took back Texas."

Trump spoke with Fox News Channel on election night, expressing surprise at several race results but also signaling a willingness to work with Democrats.

"They'll send over things that are insane, and I'll veto them," Trump said. "And after a couple of months of vetoes, they'll go out, and they'll say, ‘How do we get this stuff done?’ And we'll work together."

LIZ PEEK: THERE MAY BE A SILVER LINING IN TRUMP'S BRUTAL MIDTERM DEFEAT

Fox News Digital’s Stephen Sorace contributed to this report.

item.title: NYC's Mamdani says Abdul El-Sayed's Senate victory in Michigan 'means so much to so many'
item.description: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani praised Abdul El-Sayed's Michigan Senate win over Republican Mike Rogers, describing it as "incredibly exciting."
item.content:encoded:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Wednesday that Abdul El-Sayed's Senate election victory in Michigan "is one that means so much to so many."

El-Sayed, who will become the first Muslim U.S. senator in history, toppled former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers in what was one of the most-watched contests of the election.

"I haven't spoken to him yet. I'm sure he is quite busy. I've had the privilege of speaking to him in the past, and I have to say that his election is one that means so much to so many," Mamdani said Wednesday.

"And to see to see that victory in the face that all that he had to reckon with over the course of that campaign, whether in terms of the extraordinary amount of money spent to oppose him or the racism and slander that he was met with on a daily basis, it is incredibly exciting to see as he said last night, that the good guys won," Mamdani added.

ABDUL EL-SAYED DELIVERS MAJOR BLOW TO GOP IN MICHIGAN AFTER BRUISING SENATE RACE

Mamdani added that "what last night showed us is that Americans are tired of being told that their needs are unrealistic by politicians who have been bought by the wealthiest people in the country.

"This country has elected a new generation of leadership, a generation with a mandate to lower the cost of living, to build, not bomb, to never betray the working people who entrusted them with power," he added. "And I hear often that the politics that we're fighting for here in New York City are not possible outside of city limits. And what last night showed us is that working people are the majority, whether we are speaking of Austin or Ann Arbor or Astoria, and it is time to put those same people first in our politics and last night shows us that it's possible to do so all across the country."

STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE

Democrats regained control of the House and Senate during Tuesday's midterm elections, but Mamdani said that "it is not enough for us as Democrats to win power.

"We have to use that power to deliver change that Americans can feel in their wallets," he continued. "And to me, when you look at these campaigns, if we want to speak about James Talarico, he campaigned on a vision for universal childcare. If you want to talk about Keisha Lance Bottoms, well she campaigned on a vision of cutting red tape, to actually be able to build housing at the speed that's needed.

"If you want to talk about Jocelyn Benson, she campaigned on a moratorium for data centers. These, to me, are examples of the kind of specifics. But again, what I'm excited to see now is a recognition that the work is only just starting and that this has to be delivered for working people across the country," Mamdani declared.

item.title: Why removing your data online may still leave your family exposed

That's the problem with approaching family data broker removal one person at a time. People-search sites often connect relatives through shared addresses, public records and family relationships. In fact, the Federal Trade Commission warns that even after you opt out, your information may still appear in reports about relatives, neighbors or associates. WHY CAREFUL PEOPLE STILL END UP ON DATA BROKER SITES

Data broker profiles often contain more than one person's information. They can include family relationships that help connect individual records. Search for yourself on people-search sites such as Spokeo, Whitepages, BeenVerified or Intelius. Depending on the site and available records, you may find a section identifying possible relatives or associates.

That list could include your spouse, adult children, parents or people who once shared your address. Some connections may even be outdated or incorrect. For someone trying to learn about your household, those details can provide a starting point. Now consider what happens when you remove your own listing. Your name might disappear from the site's direct search results, but your spouse's profile could still identify you as a relative. Your parent's listing might include an address where you previously lived. As a result, removing one profile may leave behind information that points to the same person.

Family connections can create privacy gaps in several ways. Here are three examples worth checking.

Married couples often share address histories, property records and other identifying information. When one spouse removes a people-search listing, but the other remains visible, the remaining profile may still reveal their shared address, possible relatives and other household details. Some people-search reports may also include property ownership or estimated financial information, although the details vary by service. For a scammer, a spouse's publicly available information could provide another way to identify or contact someone whose direct listing has been removed.

This is one of the scenarios that concerns me most. Many adults help their parents manage online accounts and avoid scams. Yet they may overlook the personal information already available through people-search sites. An older parent's profile could include previous addresses, relatives' names and other public-record details collected over many years. That information may help criminals make a scam sound more believable. Consider the grandparent scam. Someone calls an older adult, pretends to be a grandchild facing an emergency and demands money immediately. The FTC warns that scammers may already know personal details about their targets or the family members they impersonate. Reducing publicly available information can remove some of the details criminals might use to support their stories.

The reverse can happen, too. Parents may remove their own information without checking whether their adult children have searchable profiles. A young adult's address history, voter registration information or other public records may contribute to people-search listings. Those listings can also identify possible relatives. Someone searching for that adult child could potentially discover connections to their parents and other family members. For example, a scammer might use a child's name and location to make a fake emergency call to a parent sound more credible. That's why checking only one generation of your family may leave important privacy gaps.

A SCAMMER HAS YOUR NAME, PHONE NUMBER AND ADDRESS. WHAT CAN THEY ACTUALLY DO?

Data brokers collect information from multiple sources, including public records, publicly available online information and other data brokers. Even after a successful opt-out, some information can reappear when a site obtains updated records. Meanwhile, another people-search service may still have a copy of the same details. The FTC specifically warns that opting out of people-search sites does not remove the underlying information from government public records. It also recommends checking periodically for new listings. That's why I recommend taking a household approach to personal data removal rather than concentrating on one individual.

Manually removing personal information from data broker sites takes time. Doing it for multiple family members adds even more work, especially when you have to check whether profiles have returned. Look for a service that provides ongoing removal requests, covers multiple family members and lets you track progress. While no service can erase every public record or guarantee complete removal from the internet, ongoing data removal can significantly reduce the amount of personal information available about your household. By protecting several family members together, you can help close privacy gaps that individual removals might leave behind.

Before you can reduce your household's exposure, you need to understand what information is already available.

With their knowledge and permission, search for each adult's name on several major people-search sites. Look at more than the primary profile. Check whether the listings identify relatives, current addresses or previous locations. Keep in mind that people-search databases can contain inaccurate information. A listed relationship does not automatically mean the connection is correct.

Check whether your parents or older family members have searchable profiles. If they need help, walk them through the available removal options or assist them with their permission. Pay particular attention to addresses, phone numbers and family relationships that could be useful in an impersonation scam. Also remind them to verify unexpected emergency calls by contacting family members through numbers they already know.

Adult children may have their own people-search listings, even when they have never knowingly signed up for one. Check whether those profiles reveal current addresses, previous residences or connections to other family members. Then help them understand how to request removal and why they should check again later.

After identifying exposed profiles, you can submit opt-out requests individually or use a service to manage the process. These services can automatically submit removal requests to hundreds of covered data broker and people-search sites, saving you the time and effort of handling each family member's information separately.

Because listings can reappear, look for a service that offers recurring removal requests, ongoing monitoring and progress tracking. This helps reduce the amount of personal information that strangers and scammers can find about your family. The goal is to make it harder for someone to connect individual profiles and build a detailed picture of your household.

You can spend hours cleaning up your own online profile and still have your name, address or family connections exposed through someone else's listing. That's what concerns me. Most people have no idea how much information about their families can be pieced together from publicly available records.
